service: Diagnostic laboratory test using next generation sequencing (NGS) for cancer
vignette: 69-year-old man with newly diagnosed stage IV (metastatic) non-small cell lung adenocarcinoma, with liver and bone metastases. He has decided to pursue systemic cancer treatment. His treating oncologist orders tumor tissue testing with an NGS panel that has FDA approval as a companion in vitro diagnostic with an FDA-approved indication for non-small cell lung cancer. He has never had NGS testing. The test is performed in a CLIA-certified laboratory, which returns results to the oncologist in a report template listing treatment options.
rationale_note: Metastatic NSCLC, never NGS tested, seeking chemotherapy/targeted therapy; FDA companion diagnostic indicated for NSCLC; CLIA lab; treating oncologist; report template.

service: Diagnostic laboratory test using next generation sequencing (NGS) for cancer
vignette: 71-year-old woman who underwent resection of a stage II colon adenocarcinoma 3 months ago; surveillance imaging shows no recurrence or metastasis. She wishes to receive any treatment that might help. Her treating oncologist orders tumor NGS testing with an FDA-approved companion diagnostic panel indicated for colorectal cancer, performed in a CLIA-certified laboratory with results returned in a report template listing treatment options. She has never had NGS testing.
rationale_note: Stage II colon cancer, resected, with no recurrence: not recurrent, relapsed, refractory, metastatic or stage III/IV.

service: Diagnostic laboratory test using next generation sequencing (NGS) for cancer
vignette: 64-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer whose disease has progressed on her current therapy; she has decided to pursue further treatment. Ten months ago her tumor was tested with an FDA-approved companion diagnostic NGS panel indicated for breast cancer. Her treating oncologist now orders the same NGS panel, for the same genetic content, on the same tumor tissue. The CLIA-certified laboratory would return results in a report template listing treatment options.
rationale_note: The same FDA companion diagnostic NGS test was already run on the same cancer 10 months ago; repeat for the same genetic content is not covered.

service: Diagnostic laboratory test using next generation sequencing (NGS) for cancer
vignette: 66-year-old woman with stage IIIC cutaneous melanoma who has decided to pursue systemic therapy. At diagnosis, a single-gene BRAF test using real-time PCR (not NGS) was performed. Her treating oncologist now orders tumor testing with an NGS panel that has FDA approval as a companion in vitro diagnostic with an FDA-approved indication for melanoma. She has never had NGS testing. The test is performed in a CLIA-certified laboratory, which reports to the oncologist in a template that lists treatment options.
rationale_note: Advanced stage III melanoma; a prior single-gene PCR test is a distractor because it was not the same NGS test.

service: Diagnostic laboratory test using next generation sequencing (NGS) for cancer
vignette: 58-year-old woman with breast cancer diagnosed this year. Her sister was diagnosed with ovarian cancer at age 48. Her treating oncologist documents that this family history is a risk factor for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer and that she has a clinical indication for germline testing. The oncologist orders an FDA-approved germline NGS hereditary cancer panel. She has never had germline testing. The test is performed in a CLIA-certified laboratory, which returns results to the oncologist in a report template listing treatment options.
rationale_note: Germline NGS in breast cancer with a documented clinical indication and risk factor, never previously tested; FDA-approved test, CLIA lab, report template.

service: Diagnostic laboratory test using next generation sequencing (NGS) for cancer
vignette: 67-year-old woman with recurrent high-grade serous ovarian cancer. At her original diagnosis 3 years ago she had germline testing with an FDA-approved germline NGS hereditary cancer panel, which found no pathogenic variants. Her treating oncologist documents a clinical indication and a risk factor (Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry) for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer, and orders the same germline NGS panel, for the same genetic content, again in a CLIA-certified laboratory with a report template listing treatment options.
rationale_note: Germline: the same germline NGS panel for the same content was performed 3 years ago.

service: Diagnostic laboratory test using next generation sequencing (NGS) for cancer
vignette: 70-year-old woman with newly diagnosed breast cancer. Her treating oncologist's note states 'clinical indication for germline testing' and orders an FDA-approved germline NGS hereditary cancer panel, to be run in a CLIA-certified laboratory that reports in a template listing treatment options. She has never had germline testing. The note's family history section reads 'not obtained,' and the record contains no other information about family history, ancestry, age at diagnosis, tumor features or any other risk factor for inherited breast or ovarian cancer.
rationale_note: Germline: breast cancer with a documented clinical indication, but no risk factor is documented and the family history was not taken; nothing shows absence of risk factors.

service: Diagnostic laboratory test using next generation sequencing (NGS) for cancer
vignette: 62-year-old man with metastatic colorectal cancer who has decided to pursue further chemotherapy. He has never had NGS testing. His treating oncologist sends tumor tissue for an NGS panel that has FDA approval as a companion diagnostic with an FDA-approved indication for colorectal cancer. However, the sample is sequenced at a university research laboratory that is not CLIA-certified; results would be returned to the oncologist in a report template listing treatment options.
rationale_note: All patient criteria are met, but the test is run in a research laboratory that is not CLIA-certified (required by both sections B and D).
